lessons.title: Welcoming guests and preparing your appearance
lessons.reading: しょくじのじかんをささえるむかえかたとみだしなみ

objectives.text: Use facial expressions and voice to convey a welcome
Check your appearance with food, foreign matter and odors in mind
Maintain your pre-shift appearance throughout service

sections.title: Dining is part of the stay
sections.body: In a hotel restaurant, the reassurance guests feel before sitting down and their comfort during a meal both shape the stay. Hospitality is not a matter of using many special phrases. Show a welcome through a greeting guests can notice, a clean appearance and calm movements. If staff see someone enter but continue working without acknowledging them, the guest may not know where to wait. Acknowledge the person first, then provide the guidance they need.

sections.title: A greeting and a natural expression
sections.body: Initiate the greeting yourself. Turn toward the guest and speak clearly to the end of each phrase at an audible volume. An energetic welcome does not mean shouting: in a quiet dining room, match your volume to the setting. Keep your mouth and eyes relaxed and friendly, rather than ending the interaction with an artificial smile. Watch the response after speaking to check that your guidance was understood. Friendliness and courtesy together build initial trust.

sections.title: Check hair, face and hands
sections.body: Arrange hair so it cannot touch your face or the food, and secure long hair using the facility’s method. Check any required hair net before work. Follow workplace standards for facial hair and makeup, and keep nails short and clean. Consider whether decorative nails or conspicuous nail polish are suitable for service and food handling. Do not only check your reflection: bend and reach as you would during service to check that hair or accessories do not approach the food.

sections.title: Uniform, shoes, accessories and scent
sections.body: Check your uniform for stains, creases and undone buttons, and correct how it is worn. Keep shoes clean too. Understand the manual’s general approach of avoiding accessories, and check the facility’s rules for watches and other items. Avoid strong perfume because it can affect food aromas and the comfort of others. Price is not the only consideration: items should not be conspicuous or hinder work. Correct any soiling promptly before returning to guests, rather than leaving it until the busy period.

terms.meaning: How you arrange your clothing, hair and hands with work and other people in mind
A condition that looks clean to others
The wish to receive someone warmly

example.situation: Just before entering the breakfast room, you notice hair falling across your face and an undone uniform button.
steps: Arrange your hair and uniform before entering the dining room.
Look up from your work at the entrance and greet guests first.
Observe their response, then guide them to their seats.

practice.prompt: Take turns practicing an entrance greeting and a pre-shift appearance check. Compare changing only your volume with also changing your expression and the direction you face.
expectedPoints: Face the guest and speak clearly
Check hair, nails, uniform, shoes, accessories and scent
Respond to soiling that occurs during service too

questions.prompt: What should you do first when you notice a guest at the entrance?
choices: Avoid eye contact until the guest speaks
Turn toward the guest and initiate a greeting, even if you were working
Shout at maximum volume regardless of the atmosphere
Assume a smile makes verbal guidance unnecessary
questions.explanation: First convey a welcome. Focusing only on work, excessive volume or an expression alone does not resolve the guest’s uncertainty.

questions.prompt: What should you check about long hair?
choices: It may touch food if it stays away from the face
Ignore hair that becomes loose after the initial check
Check only whether the hairstyle is fashionable
Secure it so it cannot touch the face or food during service
questions.explanation: Maintain your appearance while moving too. Preventing contact matters as well as how it looks.

questions.prompt: Your uniform is clean, but you are wearing strong perfume. What should you consider?
choices: Avoid strong scents because they affect food and other people
Scent does not matter if the uniform is clean
Expensive perfume is always acceptable
Scent cannot reach guests unless you speak to them
questions.explanation: Scent is part of the service environment. Neither price nor whether you converse determines suitability.

questions.prompt: Which combination deserves priority in a colleague’s pre-shift check?
choices: A fashionable hairstyle and an expensive watch
The perfume brand and shoe price
The condition of hair, nails and uniform, and correct dress
Only a photograph of their smile
questions.explanation: Check the specific cleanliness and clothing requirements of work involving food and guest seating.

illustration.caption: Check hair, hands, uniform and shoes in relation to movements around food.
illustration.alt: A server in a serving posture, with hair, hands, uniform and shoes marked for checking

lessons.title: Delivering food and drinks safely
lessons.reading: りょうりとのみものをあんぜんにとどける

objectives.text: Explain where to hold plates and glasses and how to set them down
Check the direction of dishes and the facility’s service method
Use basic terms for equipment and service formats

sections.title: Where to hold items and how to present them
sections.body: When serving, check not only that you will not drop the plate, but also that you do not touch the food or leave visible fingerprints. Check that your thumb is outside the plated food before carrying it. Before setting the dish down, confirm that its front faces the guest. It may look attractive to the server while still facing away from the diner. Hold a glass by its lower half rather than near the drinking rim. Set it on the table quietly so you do not interrupt conversation.

sections.title: Connect the left/right basics to local procedures
sections.body: The manual presents food from the left and drinks from the right as a basic Western-service pattern. Learn that reference, then check the seating arrangement and the facility’s actual service method. Left and right can become confusing if you think only from your own standing position. Mark the guest’s direction on a seating diagram and judge sides from there. If a narrow space prevents access from the basic side, do not force your body or the food close to guests; ask the person in charge how to proceed.

sections.title: Equipment and serving terms
sections.body: In this workplace, “silver” refers to knives, forks and similar equipment; it does not necessarily ask whether the material is silver. A caster set is a group of table condiments, so preparing tableware alone is insufficient. Haizen means carrying dishes and drinks to the table and presenting them appropriately for use. Connect the names of objects to the requested task. If asked to replenish silver, confirm which utensils and how many are missing; do not confuse it with replenishing condiments.

sections.title: Service formats and specialist staff
sections.body: A welcome drink expresses a welcome; a main dish is the central dish of the meal. At a buffet guests choose from displayed food and serve portions, whereas à la carte means ordering dishes individually. Takeout means taking the food away instead of eating in the restaurant. The same dish may require different arrangements depending on the format, so confirm the order type first. A sommelier uses specialist wine knowledge to help guests choose. Refer questions you cannot answer to the appropriate specialist rather than making claims about taste or suitability from a familiar word alone.

terms.meaning: Carrying food and drinks to guests and serving them
A workplace term for knives, forks and similar utensils
A group of table condiments
Ordering dishes individually
A specialist who uses wine knowledge to advise guests

example.situation: The dinner briefing asks you to replenish silver in the buffet room and prepare welcome drinks.
steps: Confirm the buffet format and which utensils are missing.
Replenish knives and forks, and prepare the welcoming drinks.
Check dish direction, finger position and glass handling before carrying items.

practice.prompt: Use a paper circle as a plate and an empty transparent container as a glass. Explain acceptable holding points and the front facing the guest. Then explain different service methods using seven workplace terms.
expectedPoints: Do not touch the food or drinking rim
Distinguish the left/right reference from the local procedure
Do not confuse equipment, service formats and specialist roles

questions.prompt: How should you hold a glass when serving it?
choices: Grip the drinking rim firmly
Pinch the edge
Support the lower half and set it down quietly
Put fingers inside to hide fingerprints
questions.explanation: Avoid the drinking area and hold the lower part. Setting it down quietly also shows consideration.

questions.prompt: Which viewpoint determines the front of a dish?
choices: The view of the guest who will eat it
Only the view from the kitchen exit
Only the carrying server’s view
The order in which the plate was touched
questions.explanation: Face the front toward the guest. The server’s viewpoint alone cannot determine presentation.

questions.prompt: You are told that “silver is missing.” Which preparation is most relevant?
choices: Count silver-colored room keys
Replenish takeaway bags only
Refill only the table salt
Check the number of knives, forks and similar utensils needed
questions.explanation: Here silver means knives, forks and similar items, distinct from a condiment set.

questions.prompt: What does à la carte mean?
choices: Only self-serving portions from a display of all dishes
Ordering dishes individually
A specialist wine adviser
A drink offered as a welcome
questions.explanation: Buffet, sommelier and welcome drink each have different meanings.

illustration.caption: Check the front of the dish, finger contact points and a grip away from the drinking rim.
illustration.alt: A plate showing the guest-facing side and a glass supported below its midpoint

lessons.title: Japanese meal placement and course progression
lessons.reading: わしょくのはいぜんとりょうりのながれ

objectives.text: Explain the components and basic placement of ichijū-sansai
Connect Japanese course stages to dish names
Briefly explain seasonal ingredients to guests

sections.title: Seasonality and the meal structure
sections.body: Shun describes a season when an ingredient’s characteristic quality can be enjoyed. When explaining Japanese food, do more than read dish names: ask the kitchen which ingredients express the season. Do not invent origins or harvest periods you cannot verify. Ichijū-sansai is a basic meal structure combining rice with soup and three side dishes. “Three dishes” does not mean three kinds of vegetable. Distinguishing the number of dishes from their roles also helps identify missing items.

sections.title: Placement from the diner’s viewpoint
sections.body: Decide where the diner sits before learning the layout. Place rice at the front left and soup at the front right, and use the side dish at the back left and the main dish at the back right as basic reference points. The manual’s layout teaches the basics; it does not fix every item in every meal to an identical place. Check the actual menu and the facility’s serving example for the correct number and orientation. Do not reverse left and right by looking only from the server’s side.

sections.title: Recognize dishes in the first half of a course
sections.body: The manual’s Japanese course example progresses through appetizer, wanmori, sashimi and grilled dish. Connect names with actual dishes: an appetizer opens the meal, wanmori is served in a bowl, and otsukuri is a presentation such as sliced fish. Being able to name the next dish or vessel is more useful in work than memorizing numbers alone. This order is one example in the manual and varies by facility and menu. Check the planned progression rather than rearranging the actual menu based only on a name.

sections.title: Prepare with the later courses in mind
sections.body: The example continues with simmered food, fried food, a vinegared dish, rice and pickles, then mizugashi. Kōnomono means pickles, while mizugashi in this context means fruit or a similar ending to the meal; do not infer a water-filled sweet from its name. Knowing the progression helps prepare the next plate and clear used vessels. However, do not remove food still being eaten just because the next course is due. Support the whole meal in line with the guests’ progress and the person in charge.

terms.meaning: A basic meal structure of rice, soup and three dishes
The season when an ingredient’s characteristic quality can be enjoyed
A dish presented in a bowl
Pickles
Fruit or a similar ending to a Japanese meal

example.situation: While preparing a ryokan dinner, you view the serving example from the opposite side and become unsure where rice and soup belong.
steps: Mark the diner’s direction on paper.
Confirm rice on the left and soup on the right from that viewpoint.
Check the day’s menu and order with the person in charge, matching names to vessels.

practice.prompt: Draw the ichijū-sansai layout and explain the nine stages of the manual’s Japanese course example. Also explain what to check if the day’s menu differs.
expectedPoints: Judge left and right from the diner’s viewpoint
Three dishes means three accompaniments
Do not turn one example into the only workplace rule

questions.prompt: What does “three dishes” in ichijū-sansai mean?
choices: A requirement to use only three kinds of vegetable
Soup for three people
Three accompaniments
Food stored for three days
questions.explanation: Ichijū-sansai describes a meal composition, not vegetable types, guest numbers or storage duration.

questions.prompt: Where are rice and soup in the basic layout from the diner’s viewpoint?
choices: Rice left, soup right
Both at the back right
Rice right, soup left
Use only the server’s left side
questions.explanation: Use the guest’s orientation; it differs from that of a server standing opposite.

questions.prompt: In the manual’s Japanese course example, what follows sashimi?
choices: Fruit
Pickles
Coffee
Grilled food
questions.explanation: The example begins with appetizer, bowl dish, sashimi and grilled food. Check the actual menu at work.

questions.prompt: The day’s course order differs from the manual’s example. What should you do?
choices: Ask guests to eat again in the manual’s order
Check the facility’s menu and progression with the person in charge
Change the order without permission using the manual
Skip the check because names do not matter
questions.explanation: Understand the basic example, then prepare for the actual menu and progression.

illustration.caption: Check rice, soup, main and side-dish placement from the guest’s viewpoint.
illustration.alt: An overhead Japanese meal layout with the guest seated at the bottom

lessons.title: Western tableware and consideration for food cultures
lessons.reading: ようしょくのどうぐとしょくぶんかへのはいりょ

objectives.text: Read basic Western placement and in-progress/finished signals
Ask about cultural differences without assumptions
Connect halal and vegetarian terminology to confirmation

sections.title: Course progression and equipment placement
sections.body: The manual’s Western course example progresses through hors d’oeuvre, soup, fish, meat, dessert and coffee. Menus vary, but the sequence helps plan preparations from beginning to end. Around the plate, use forks on the left, knives and spoons on the right, dessert utensils above and the bread plate at the upper left as basic positions. When there are many utensils, check their use order and placement rather than symmetry alone. Replenish missing equipment before the dish arrives so there is no last-minute rush.

sections.title: Use order and dining signals
sections.body: The basic approach described is a knife in the right hand and a fork in the left. Use multiple utensils from the outside inward. A separated, inverted-V arrangement on the plate indicates eating is in progress, while parallel utensils toward the lower right suggest the meal is finished. Do not decide every guest’s intention from placement alone. Politely asking before clearing avoids taking a plate the guest still wants. Use manners as clues for smooth service, not to judge guests.

sections.title: Confirm what the guest can eat
sections.body: Food habits differ by country, culture and personal outlook. Halal concerns what is permitted under Islamic teachings and requires checking food and preparation methods. Pork-derived ingredients and alcohol matter, but their absence alone does not prove every dish is halal-suitable. Vegetarian also does not mean everyone eats exactly the same foods. Rather than deciding from the label, ask which ingredients the guest avoids and what conditions need checking, then provide information confirmed with the kitchen.

sections.title: Explain what you do not yet know
sections.body: Recommending an unverified dish as “probably fine” can damage trust. Separate confirmed facts from what remains unknown. Say, “May I check the ingredients with the kitchen? Thank you for waiting,” then report the result. Explain honestly if some conditions cannot be accommodated. Do not pressure the guest to eat the same meal as others; provide accurate information for their choice. If you cannot answer alone, involve the manager or knowledgeable staff.

terms.meaning: Knives, forks and spoons used for eating
An appetizer served at the beginning of a Western course
A term for what is permitted in Islamic teachings
A name for plant-centered food habits; confirm the person’s specific conditions

example.situation: A guest says they do not eat meat. A staff member assumes a soup is suitable because no meat is visible.
steps: Ask which foods and conditions need checking.
Confirm the soup’s actual ingredients with the kitchen.
Explain verified information and the facility’s limits so the guest can choose.

practice.prompt: Draw a Western place setting and explain utensil order and meal signals. Then describe what to check when asked “Is this halal?” or told “I avoid meat.”
expectedPoints: Explain the layout from the guest’s viewpoint
Use signals as clues and confirm completion
Do not decide ingredients or suitability from a cultural label alone

questions.prompt: What is the basic order for multiple utensils?
choices: Inside first
Outside first
Most expensive first
Largest first
questions.explanation: The basic order is outside inward, not by size or price.

questions.prompt: Two utensils are aligned toward the lower right. What is appropriate?
choices: Treat it as a possible finish signal and ask before clearing
Assume eating must still be in progress and never respond
Scold the guest and reposition them
Ignore intention and clear every plate immediately
questions.explanation: The arrangement suggests completion, but confirm the guest’s intention before clearing.

questions.prompt: How should you recommend a dish with no visible meat to a vegetarian guest?
choices: Guarantee it from appearance alone
Ask them to eat the same food as everyone else
Assume all people using the label have identical conditions
Confirm their conditions and the actual ingredients
questions.explanation: Appearance may not reveal ingredients. Confirm both the person’s needs and the kitchen’s information.

questions.prompt: You have confirmed only that pork and alcohol are not used. What should you say?
choices: Claim every certification is present
Guarantee suitability for every possible condition
Explain the confirmed ingredient information and check unverified conditions
Label it halal-certified without checking
questions.explanation: Do not guarantee certifications or preparation conditions that have not been confirmed.

illustration.caption: Distinguish equipment placement and utensil arrangements during and after eating.
illustration.alt: A place setting with fork left, knife and spoon right, bread plate upper left and dessert utensils above

lessons.title: Connecting allergy information with hygiene
lessons.reading: あれるぎーじょうほうとえいせいをつなぐ

objectives.text: Explain allergy risks and the need to share information
Check foods whose ingredients are not visible
Explain handwashing and separation of raw foods

sections.title: Do not judge safety from a small quantity
sections.body: A food allergy causes symptoms in response to a trigger food. Severe reactions may affect breathing and can be life-threatening. Do not treat an allergy like a preference: confirm whether an allergy exists and which foods are involved at booking or arrival. If only the staff member who heard it remembers, another server may make an error. Match the person, ingredient and dish accurately, and share that information with the kitchen and service staff. Do not personally promise that a small amount is safe.

sections.title: Ingredients not apparent from appearance
sections.body: Egg, milk, wheat, peanuts and seafood are among ingredients whose presence may not be clear from a dish name. Wheat may be in bread and noodles, but also coatings, wrappers, breadcrumbs and some condiments. Do not assume every soy sauce or miso has the same ingredients: check the actual products and recipe. The manual’s ingredient examples prompt checks; they are not the latest legal list of mandatory labels. Verify current official rules separately before stating statutory counts or revision dates to guests.

sections.title: Hands and food handling
sections.body: Wash hands before and after food handling and after using the toilet. Understand the purpose and procedure for washing and hand disinfection, and follow the facility’s method. Do not assume alcohol makes handwashing unnecessary. Store each food at suitable temperatures and conditions, and separate raw meat and fish from other foods. Do not invent temperatures or times from a source that gives no numerical conditions. Check the hygiene procedure and ask the responsible person before working with unfamiliar storage requirements.

sections.title: Keep the check before serving
sections.body: Even if the dish was checked for suitability, delivery to the wrong table defeats information-sharing. Match the guest and dish at ordering, preparation and service. If a point remains unclear, do not guess because service is busy; check with the responsible staff. Hygiene is not limited to opening time. Washing at task changes, separating foods and maintaining cleanliness support both a comfortable meal and food-poisoning prevention.

terms.reading: しょくもつあれるぎー
terms.meaning: Symptoms caused by a reaction to a particular food
Materials used to make a food or dish
Ensuring responsible people have the same necessary information

example.situation: A guest who reported a wheat allergy orders a dish with sauce. The menu name does not mention wheat.
steps: Confirm and record the trigger ingredient and the guest concerned.
Ask the kitchen to check products and recipes, including sauce and coatings.
Share the results and match the dish to the intended guest before service.

practice.prompt: Explain what is unverified when someone says, “There is no wheat in the dish name, so it is safe.” Then name three task changes requiring handwashing.
expectedPoints: Check condiments, coatings and wrappers too
Do not guarantee safety alone; share with the kitchen
Continue handwashing and appropriate storage

questions.prompt: The dish name does not mention wheat. What should you do?
choices: Guarantee it is wheat-free
Check actual ingredients and the recipe
Do not check condiments
Guarantee safety after removing the coating
questions.explanation: A name does not reveal condiments. Neither appearance nor removing one part establishes safety.

questions.prompt: What is needed after receiving an allergy report?
choices: Have only the listener remember it
Check appearance alone
Share the trigger, person and dish with kitchen and service staff
Wait until the next visit before passing it on
questions.explanation: Connect the person and dish so information is not lost between preparation and service.

questions.prompt: Which handwashing approach is appropriate?
choices: Alcohol alone replaces washing even after toilet use
One wash at opening lasts until closing
Decide only by a daily count, not task changes
Wash before/after food handling and after toilet use using the facility’s procedure
questions.explanation: Wash according to tasks and exposure opportunities. A count alone or disinfection alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: How should raw meat and fish be stored?
choices: Under appropriate food-specific conditions, separate from other foods
In one container without checking temperature
Anywhere space is available
Ignore temperature if the manual supplies no number
questions.explanation: Use suitable conditions and separation. Ask the responsible person or consult procedures for unknown temperatures.

illustration.caption: Keep the reported ingredient information connected through booking, preparation and service.
illustration.alt: The same guest identifier and ingredient marker matched on a reservation, kitchen check and serving slip

lessons.title: Maintaining cleanliness from opening to closing
lessons.reading: かいてんからへいてんまでせいけつをたもつ

objectives.text: Match dining-room and kitchen preparations before opening
Connect closing tasks with next-day readiness
Explain how cleaning and food handling prevent food poisoning

sections.title: Check the whole room before opening
sections.body: Clean the entrance and dining room, prepare sufficient tableware and supplies, and organize them. Check the combination of napkins, tableware, cutlery and condiment sets. Tables and chairs require not only arrangement but wiping according to the facility’s method. Attractive visible tables are not enough if the entrance is dirty or supplies are missing: service may stop after opening. Even when duties are divided, make a final overall check rather than assuming someone else completed an item.

sections.title: Connect food and guest information
sections.body: Alongside room preparation, confirm the day’s dishes and guest information with the kitchen. Do not open after checking only seat numbers while remaining unaware of changed dishes or special considerations. Ensure staff share menu explanations, service arrangements and reported dietary needs. Do not mark an unchecked item complete. Ask the responsible person before opening to reduce situations where staff learn important information for the first time at the table and rush it to the kitchen.

sections.title: Hand closing work to the next shift
sections.body: After all guests leave, clean the entrance and dining room, and replenish and organize tableware and supplies. Check condiment sets for cleaning as well as quantity, and arrange and wipe tables and chairs. Dispose of waste appropriately and keep next-day work areas clean. Closing is not simply a race to leave after clearing up. Distinguish completed from outstanding tasks in the handover so the next shift does not start by searching for missing items and dirt.

sections.title: Maintain hygiene continuously
sections.body: Cleaning does not end with a checkmark at opening or closing. Respond to soiling during service using the facility’s method and maintain cleanliness. Food poisoning can involve bacteria, viruses and parasites; the manual gives norovirus, Campylobacter and Salmonella as examples. Connect these names to handwashing, food separation, appropriate storage and ongoing cleaning. Do not assume prevention matters in only one season. For meat and fish storage or thawing, check procedures that prevent released liquid from spreading to other food.

terms.meaning: Preparing the room, supplies and food information before service
Adding missing items to restore the required amount
Liquid released from meat or fish
Unwanted material to be disposed of by the facility’s method

example.situation: At closing, dishes have been cleared, but condiment sets remain dirty and underfilled. A different shift opens the next morning.
steps: Clean and replenish the condiment sets.
Check the entrance, seating, supplies and waste as well.
Describe any unfinished tasks clearly in the next-shift handover.

practice.prompt: Make separate opening and closing checklists. Explain shared items and distinguish the pre-opening check of dishes and guest information.
expectedPoints: Preparation includes supplies, settings and information as well as cleaning
Check replenishment and waste disposal after closing
Connect ongoing cleaning to appropriate food handling

questions.prompt: What is needed before opening besides cleaning guest seating?
choices: Present yesterday’s menu unchanged
Confirm today’s food and guest information with the kitchen
Leave shortages until guests arrive
Mark everything complete before checking
questions.explanation: Dishes and guest information are part of opening preparation. Appearance alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Which closing action is appropriate?
choices: Leave condiment sets untouched until next week after clearing plates
Ask the next guest to replenish everything
Clear all tables while guests are still eating
After guests leave, check cleaning, replenishment, condiment cleaning and waste disposal
questions.explanation: Closing supports next-day readiness. Check washing, replenishing, organization and disposal.

questions.prompt: Which approach to food-poisoning prevention is appropriate?
choices: Causes include bacteria and viruses, so maintain daily handwashing, storage and cleaning
Clean only in winter
Memorizing pathogen names replaces food separation
Ignore service-time dirt if cleaning was done before opening
questions.explanation: Names must be connected to everyday hygiene, not memorized in place of action.

questions.prompt: What should you do about liquid from meat or fish during storage and thawing?
choices: Ignore storage conditions if it is not red
Put all foods together so the liquid reaches them
Check a method that prevents liquid spreading to other foods
Leave released liquid without telling anyone
questions.explanation: Handle released liquid as part of food separation and the facility’s storage/thawing procedure.

illustration.caption: Before and after service, check seating, supplies and kitchen information together.
illustration.alt: A comparison of pre-opening tables and the cleaning/replenishment points after closing

lessons.title: Observing tables and meeting requests as a team
lessons.reading: きゃくせきをかんさつしちーむでようぼうにこたえる

objectives.text: Infer possible service needs from changes and confirm the guest’s wishes
Prepare seating and support that match an individual guest’s needs
Connect complaints with reporting, improvement and staff guidance

sections.title: Turn small changes into action
sections.body: At level 2, coordinate the whole room as well as completing your own tasks. Notice finished plates, empty glasses, guests seeking another order or dropped utensils. When you infer a need, confirm the guest’s wishes before clearing, topping up or asking about another order. Replace dropped utensils promptly. Separate what you observed from what the guest actually wants; otherwise anticipation can become an imposition.

sections.title: Ask the person what support is needed
sections.body: Wheelchair use, pregnancy, older age, disability or religious circumstances can create diverse needs. People with the same background do not necessarily want the same help. Listen carefully and confirm the assistance before acting. Review reservations and consider routes and space when assigning tables. Ask whether being near an entrance is preferable too. If seating assistance is requested, move the chair slowly and quietly, using actions that help the guest feel secure.

sections.title: Do not handle complaints alone
sections.body: Listen to what happened and what is troubling the guest without deciding prematurely. Apologize courteously for the unpleasant experience and report to a superior so an appropriate response can follow. Even a seemingly small problem should not be handled independently without reporting. Separate immediate actions from matters requiring a decision; do not promise unconfirmed outcomes. Managers should also identify which explanation or handover caused the problem and use it to guide staff and prevent recurrence.

sections.title: Coordinate the whole operation as manager
sections.body: Managers oversee food, service, hygiene, guest care and complaints together. Staff education and customer management also require reducing situations where only one person holds information. If seating changes, communicate what the serving staff need to know. Instead of telling a newcomer only to “be more attentive,” specify what to observe, when to ask the guest and whom to inform. Combine respect for the person with a system the team can actually carry out.

terms.meaning: Assigning tables with reservation information and guest wishes in mind
Removing tableware after use
Considering the person’s circumstances and wishes when responding

example.situation: A wheelchair user is directed to an entrance-side table without being asked, but requests a quiet table farther inside.
steps: Acknowledge the assumption and ask about wishes and required support.
Check available tables and routes, explaining the choices.
Tell service staff the changed location and review future guidance with the team.

practice.prompt: Discuss three situations: an empty glass, a dropped fork and a complaint about seating. Explain observation, guest confirmation, action and reporting for each.
expectedPoints: Observation alone does not establish wishes
Confirm support with the guest
Report complaints and connect them to team improvement

questions.prompt: What is appropriate when you notice an empty glass?
choices: Assume the same drink must be wanted
Confirm wishes and ask about another order
No observation is necessary
Replace it with an expensive drink without asking
questions.explanation: A change prompts a question; confirm wishes before responding.

questions.prompt: How should seating be prepared for a wheelchair user?
choices: Assume everyone prefers the entrance
Do not speak to the person
Check reservation information, wishes, route and space
Ignore the person and rely only on a companion
questions.explanation: A background does not determine preferences. Confirm support with the guest.

questions.prompt: What should you do with a seemingly minor complaint?
choices: Handle it alone without a record or report
Argue without listening
Hide it from a superior
Listen, apologize and report to a superior to respond
questions.explanation: The manual calls for reporting even small issues. Concealment and independent decisions are inappropriate.

questions.prompt: Which manager’s instruction to a newcomer is specific?
choices: When you notice a dropped utensil, prepare a clean replacement and speak to the guest
Repeat only the word attentiveness
Tell them not to report complaints
Tell them to watch food but ignore hygiene
questions.explanation: Specifying the observation and action supports overall management and staff education.

illustration.caption: Choose a table by combining the guest’s wishes with routes and available space.
illustration.alt: A wheelchair user, several tables, entrance routes and a staff member confirming preferences

lessons.title: Managing beverage recommendations and varied dietary needs
lessons.reading: いんりょうていあんとたようなしょくじじょうけんをかんりする

objectives.text: Confirm preferences and the menu before recommending a drink
Explain basic sake and wine terminology
Verify and communicate regional, seasonal and cultural food information

sections.title: Begin recommendations by asking preferences
sections.body: To recommend a drink with food, check the menu and the guest’s preferences together. Getting a guest to buy a more expensive item is not the sole purpose. Ask what type they would like, explain differences and propose options at a suitable moment. Pairing can affect satisfaction and sales, but do not impose an unwanted order. Ask a sommelier or knowledgeable colleague about features you cannot explain. Accept a refusal pleasantly and keep the meal flowing.

sections.title: Explain sake
sections.body: Understand rice, kōji and water as the principal ingredients of seishu sake. Regional brands offer different products, and chilled, room-temperature and warmed sake are different serving states. Do not assume all products are served at the same temperature: check the product and facility’s method. Do not infer sweetness from a local origin alone. Ask preferences and explain verified features and serving states. Knowing basic ingredients does not guarantee suitability for a dietary condition; check the particular product when needed.

sections.title: Organize wine names
sections.body: Examples of red-wine grapes in the manual are Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir and Syrah; white examples include Chardonnay, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc. Distinguish grape names from regions. Bordeaux and Burgundy are French examples, and California is an American example. Do not promise a pairing from red or white alone: check the actual menu and product. Instead of reciting a memorized explanation, give concise information that answers the guest’s question.

sections.title: Check local sourcing and dietary conditions
sections.body: Local production for local consumption means using regional agricultural or fishery products locally, and complements explanations of seasonal menus. Check where the served ingredients actually come from before describing them. Halal considerations may involve ingredients, alcohol, preparation and verifiable certification, rather than only avoiding pork. Vegetarian conditions differ by person; vegan approaches also avoid animal products including eggs and dairy. Do not answer from a label alone: match requested conditions, products and the facility’s actual capability.

lessons.title: Using figures to manage sales, food cost and staffing
lessons.reading: うりあげげんかじんいんをすうじでかんがえる

objectives.text: Calculate food-cost and FL ratios using figures from the same period
Explain F&B control and ABC analysis
Choose improvements using service quality as well as ratios

sections.title: Distinguish profit from expenses
sections.body: A restaurant manager considers sales, expenses and operating profit while maintaining service. Higher sales do not mean equivalent profit growth if costs rise more. The manual lists food cost, labor, selling/administrative expenses and utilities. Check the establishment’s accounting method so the same cost is not counted twice under different headings. Do not call the amount remaining after food and labor alone operating profit: other operating expenses must be considered too.

sections.title: Calculate the food-cost ratio
sections.body: Food-cost ratio (%) = food cost for the same period ÷ sales × 100. For monthly sales of ¥2,000,000 and food cost of ¥640,000, 64 ÷ 200 × 100 = 32%, using units of ¥10,000. Converting both amounts to yen gives the same result. If sales are zero, the ratio cannot be calculated with this formula; do not force a record of 0%. The manual’s 30% target is a management example to consider by business type and product mix, not a universal legal requirement.

sections.title: FL ratio and its scope
sections.body: FL ratio (%) = (food cost + labor cost) ÷ sales × 100. With sales of ¥2,000,000, food of ¥640,000 and labor of ¥520,000, (64 + 52) ÷ 200 × 100 = 58%. Do not confuse it with the 32% food-cost ratio. Distinguish percentages from decimals: 58% is 0.58 when used as a factor. The manual’s guideline of 60% or less is not a duty for every business. Because other costs exist, a 58% FL ratio does not establish a 42% profit margin.

sections.title: F&B control and ABC analysis
sections.body: F&B control checks food and beverage quality, purchase quantities and prices, sales, stock and food loss. Simply buying cheaper items can reduce quality and satisfaction. ABC analysis classifies menu items using a chosen measure such as sales or profit to identify priorities for management. Record the measure and period, rather than making rankings alone. The item with the highest sales need not produce the most profit; choose figures that fit the purpose.

questions.prompt: Monthly sales are ¥1,800,000 and food cost ¥540,000. What is the food-cost ratio?
questions.explanation: 54 ÷ 180 × 100 = 30%. Match the reporting period and money units.

questions.prompt: Monthly sales are ¥1,800,000, food cost ¥540,000 and labor ¥630,000. What is the FL ratio?
questions.explanation: (54 + 63) ÷ 180 × 100 = 65%. Include labor as well as food cost.

questions.prompt: How should the manual’s 30% and 60% guidelines be treated?
choices: As laws binding every establishment
As a reason to ignore other costs when below them
As proof that the remaining FL percentage is operating profit
As management references dependent on the business, not universal legal duties
questions.explanation: Distinguish guidance from law. Other costs mean the remainder is not automatically profit.

questions.prompt: Sales and profit give different ABC rankings. What should you do?
choices: State the measure and period that fit the analysis purpose
Assume the highest-selling item always has the highest profit
Ignore quality and stock entirely
Remove every product based on ranking alone
questions.explanation: Choose a measure suited to the management purpose and consider quality and stock alongside F&B control.
